list.listitem: Initiate cooling immediately in any patient suspected of heatstroke. Rapid recognition and treatment of heat stroke is essential to controlling morbidity and mortality. C
Consider other causes of pyrexia and mental status change in heatstroke patients. C
Community-based heat education and heat shelters are proven to decrease mortality in at-risk populations. B

background.definition: Heatstroke is a medical emergency involving both hyperthermia and mental status change. Heatstroke can be encountered as a result of chronic heat stress in its classic form or acutely as a result of exertion, sometimes combined with exogenous heat loading.

list.listitem: Heatstroke incidence: 0.2 cases per 1000 persons per year
Heat-related deaths: 240 annually in the United States
Heatstroke mortality: third leading cause of mortality in athletes during physical activity.
Extremes of temperature.
Medications that compromise thermoregulatory mechanisms.
Environmental conditions (firefighters, etc.).
Exertion.
Aging.
Lack of acclimatization.
Recent research has identified possible genetic susceptibility related to ryanodine receptor type 1 variants similar to those seen with malignant hyperthermia.
Heat is exchanged with the environment through conduction, convection, radiation, and evaporation.
Evaporation is the most effective form of heat transfer under most conditions.
Effective evaporation requires temperature and humidity gradients; evaporation is compromised in environments with decreased gradients or with certain types of clothing.
High levels of cardiopulmonary fitness can improve tolerance of heat stress.
Extrinsic and intrinsic factors can overwhelm the body's ability to exchange heat, and core temperature increases.

The "2 hit hypothesis" posits that initial stimulus (e.g., mild illness or infection, allergic reaction, etc.) increases vulnerability to subsequent heat stress and results in development of heatstroke.
Cellular destruction, release of endotoxins and inflammatory factors, and multisystem failure occur if the hyperthermia remains unchecked.

"Leaky gut" hypothesis suggests that intestinal wall permiability increases under exercise and especially heat stress conditions, causing release of bacteria and endotoxins and leading to damage and sometime shutdown of reticuloendothelial system.
Consider screening patients involved in high-risk occupations. B

Patients should train and work only under appropriate conditions; advise patients to allow 7 to 14 days for heat acclimation and to refrain from working or training in the heat when ill or dehydrated.C
Early warning, community collaboration, and intervention programs decrease morbidity and mortality associated with heat. Radio broadcasts can effectively alert populations to heat danger. B
Fans alone are inadequate to prevent classic heatstroke. Access to air conditioning is critical for at-risk populations. B
The American College of Sports Medicine recommends no exercise for 7 days after a heatstroke event, with gradual return to excercise over 2 to 4 weeks under supervision.
Heat stress testing can aid in stratifying risk for subsequent heatstroke. This is utilized primarily among exertional heatstroke victims.
Test involves exercising under conditions of high heat and humidity with continuous core temperature monitoring.
Consider heatstroke in patients with core temperature >40°C. C
Heatstroke diagnosis rests on the observation of hyperthermia and CNS involvement. C
Exclude other causes of CNS dysfunction. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Insidious course, elevated thyroid hormone level

list.listitem: Symptoms of heatstroke can include anhydrosis, palpitations due to cardiac arrhythmias, hyperpyrexia, hyperventilation, and mental status changes.
Symptoms may also arise from complications, including cardiac arrhythmias, disseminated intravascular coagulation, hepatic failure, pulmonary edema, renal failure, rhabdomyolysis, and shock.
Symptoms of heatstroke do not follow a typical pattern; any or all may occur with a given patient.
Initial assessment should include evaluation for comorbid conditions and medications that may affect the ability to thermoregulate.

Core temperature should be measured as part of the initial survey. Heatstroke is likely if core temperature is >40°C. Rectal and esophageal probe are the most accurate and practical means for measuring core temperature. Ingestible tablets are a promising emerging technology in temperature assessment.
Hepatic profile and renal function should be assessed (ALT/AST >1000 IU/L is common).
Clotting studies should be obtained for investigation of possible disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC).
Elevated creatinine kinase (CK) may indicate rhabdomyolysis; values of 10,000 to 100,000 IU/L are common.
Blood and urine toxicology screening as well as blood glucose levels may indicate other causes for mental status changes. MDMA and other recreational drugs are an emerging source of heatstroke risk.
White blood count and sedimentation rate (ESR) may help rule out infection.
Arterial blood gas (ABG) will identify acidosis resulting from organ failure and shock.

Evaluate for significant CNS involvement (e.g., irritability, confusion, coma). If CNS impairment and hyperthermia are observed, diagnosis of heatstroke is likely. Activate emergency medical services (EMS), and follow ATLS protocols.

Obtain means of continuous core temperature monitoring. Tympanic, oral, or skin temperature readings are insufficient for diagnosis or monitoring of treatment. Suspect heatstroke if core temperature is >40°C.
Rectal thermistor monitoring is most common. Probes should be inserted to 15 cm (6 in) depth.
Initiate cooling in the field without delay, and arrange immediate transfer to medical facility.

In the field, guidelines from the Wilderness Medical Society recommend that milder forms of heat related illness (HRI) can be treated by oral fluid replacement, removal from heat source, and passive cooling. Moderate forms should be treated additionally with active cooling, such as evaporative and convective cooling (fanning/misting). Severe forms of HRI should be treated with all of the above, plus conductive cooling (ice/cold water immersion) with evacuation to a hospital for further treatment.
Initiate cooling rapidly to prevent long-term sequelae of heatstroke. C
Antipyretic medications are not effective in treating heatstroke. C
Guidelines from the Wilderness Medical Society recommend that milder forms of heat related illness (HRI) can be treated by oral fluid replacement, removal from heat source, and passive cooling. C
Moderate forms should be treated additionally with active cooling, such as evaporative and convective cooling (fanning/misting). C

Muscle relaxants such as benzodiazepines and neuroleptic agents such as chlorpromazine (Thorazine) have been employed to inhibit shivering and as a prophylaxis against seizures. However, no clinical trials have demonstrated their efficacy.
Antipyretic agents have not been shown to be effective in patients with heatstroke.
Hepatic damage may make acetaminophen inadvisable in these patients.

Rapid cooling is essential to survival and recovery. Immersion likely achieves the most rapid rates of field-based cooling. Immersion cooling can be achieved in a shallow ice bath. Even delayed immersion is likely to be efffective based on physiologic simulations. If not possible, immersion in tepid water may produce cooling rates similar to those achieved with ice water.
Dampened blankets combined with ice packs to the groin, axilla neck and head are an alternative means of cooling when immersion is not feasible.

Core afterdrop with resultant hypothermia is common, so active cooling should be discontinued before the patient is normothermic. While no evidence exists to indicate an optimal temperature, most experts suggest that discontinuation of cooling at or below core temperatures of 39°C is generally safe.

Evaporative cooling is also widely used, though cooling rates may be inferior to immersion. In this technique, a mist of cool water (15°C [45°F]) is sprayed on the patient's skin while air is fanned over the body. No studies directly comparing evaporative and immersion methods of cooling currently exist.
Evaporative cooling may be preferred in the elderly or those who may need greater monitoring or resuscitative efforts.

Internal cooling methods (cardiopulmonary bypass, gastric, bladder and rectal cold water lavage, peritoneal and thoracic lavage) are also utilized in extreme circumstances and can achieve the most rapid rates of cooling.
Prehospital cold saline infusion associated with reduced hospital days, faster normalization of hepatic function, and lower peak creatinine levels.

Wilderness Medical Society guidelines are summarized below: Mild heat related illness (HRI): Rehydrate orally; use elevation and compression for edema. Moderate HRI: For heat syncope, remove the patient from heat, use passive cooling (loosen/remove clothing, find shade), and provide oral rehydration. For heat exhaustion, use intravenous hydration and evaporative and convective cooling (facilitating air movement over the exposed or loosely clothed body, such as fanning and misting). Chemical cold packs or ice packs can assist in cooling, but are best on a large (entire body) scale. Ice towels are not very effective. Antipyretics should be avoided as they do not cool the patient. Severe HRI: For severe HRI, such as exertional heat stroke, remove from heat source; address ABCs; provide conductive cooling (via cold water or ice water immersion), evaporative cooling, and convective cooling; provide intravenous hydration; and evacuate to a hospital. Intravenous hydration is recommended for patients with altered mental status. Do not delay cooling to provide hydration. Exercise-associated hyponatremia can present similarly to heat exhaustion and heat stroke. Treatment for heat stroke should not be delayed based on a diagnostic threshold of a temperature of 40°C.
Hospitalize patients for at least 48 hours after heatstroke.
Serial laboratory monitoring for 48 hours is essential. Consider serologic monitoring for 96 hours, and up to 16 days in patients with elevated muscle enzymes or liver function-associated markers.
Duration of cooling: the Wilderness Medical Society guidelines recommend stopping active cooling at 38.3°C to 38.9°C to prevent hypothermic overshoot.

Most patients with heatstroke should be referred for monitoring in a hospital emergency department. Recent evidence suggests that many patients with heat related illness who are rapidly diagnosed and cooled and are clinically stable can safely be discharged home with family.
Critical care or environmental specialist consultation should be obtained.

Supervised return to activity should be performed before releasing heatstroke victims to unrestricted work and exercise in the heat. Conside heat stress testing for those who remain symptomatic when exposed to heat stress after 2 to 4 weeks.C

In one follow-up study of 83 urban patients who suffered heatstroke following a heat wave in France, 28-day and 2-year mortality rates were 58% and 71%, respectively. Mortality was associated with coming from an institution (hazard ratio [HR] 2.0; 95% CI, 1.0-3.7), use of long-term antihypertensive medication (HR 2.2; 95% CI, 1.2-4.1), anuria at presentation (HR 5.2; 95% CI, 2.3-12), coma (HR 3.0; 95% CI, 1.3-6.9), and cardiovascular failure (HR 2.4; 95% CI, 1.1-5.2).
Predictors of hospitalization in a Japanese study included age 65 years and older, increasing body temperature, abnormal Glasgow Coma Score, and elevated serum creatinine.
A review of 994 hospitalizations for heat stroke in US Army personnel (34% younger than 21 years) founda 3.7% mortality rate and a 25% rate of rhabdomyolysis.
Survival approaches 100% in patients who are cooled promptly. B
Core temperature rapidly rises, causing disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), shock, multisystem failure, and death. Permanent CNS injury occurs in 20% of cases. B
Schedule follow-up for elderly patients or patients with mental health conditions that might place them at greater risk for recurrence.
Ensure that elderly patients have access to air conditioning and to media sources that might alert them to heat danger.

Excessive heat is teratogenic in pregnancy; advise pregnant women to employ good temperature regulatory strategies to avoid overheating while exercising. Adequate hydration and use of cool, light clothing are recommended.
